knowledge_type_note: Motif (D). Informant theme h. Recognition is heuristic — it depends on the follow-up.
definition_short: Luring an enemy piece ONTO a square where a tactic works against it.
definition_long:
Usually a sacrifice that the opponent must accept, dragging the king or a piece onto a fork square, a mating square, or a line where a pin or skewer becomes available. Where deflection removes a defender, a decoy positions a victim.

The classic form is a check or capture offered on a square adjacent to a knight fork, or a queen sacrifice that pulls the king onto an open line.

history.notes: Tactical motifs are descriptive pattern names of long and mostly anonymous usage. The Chess Informant classification is cited as a standard enumeration, not as the origin of the term.

preconditions: A forcing offer exists that the opponent must or will accept
Accepting places an enemy unit on a square where a further tactic works
indicators_for: The lured square is a fork square, a mating square, or on a line with another target
The offer is a check, so acceptance is forced
indicators_against: The offer can be declined without cost
The follow-up tactic does not actually exist after the capture
The lured piece can immediately step away with tempo

typical_plans: Find the square where a fork, a mate or a skewer would already work, then look for a way to force an enemy piece onto it
Against a castled king, check on a square adjacent to a knight's forking square
In the endgame, decoy the defending king one square away from the queening square rather than one square towards you
typical_moves: A queen sacrifice on h8 or g8 pulling the king onto a square a knight covers
A check that must be answered by a capture, where the capturing piece lands on a pinned line
A pawn push offering itself so the capturing pawn blocks its own defender
typical_piece_arrangements: A knight two moves from a fork whose forking square is empty
An enemy king on an open rank or file with a heavy piece able to arrive on it
tactical_consequences: The decoying move is almost always a check or a capture, because the victim has to be forced rather than invited

Decoy and deflection are the same sacrifice read differently: deflection removes a defender from a duty, decoy puts a victim on a square. A single move is often both, and this base does not try to choose between them

exceptions: A decoy fails outright if the sacrifice can be declined.
A decoy that lands the enemy king on a square where the follow-up needs one more move than the defender has is not a decoy, it is a lost piece.
Decoying a defender onto a square where it still defends is the commonest miscalculation in this motif.
limitations: Only identifiable by looking at the resulting position, so it cannot be detected from the move alone.

NO VERIFIED POSITION HAS BEEN BUILT FOR THIS RECORD. Four constructions were tried and each failed for the same reason: the Damiano and Anastasia shapes that make a clean decoy need a specific queen-and-knight geometry with the h-file already open, and every minimal version either mated without the decoy or left the sacrificing side simply a queen down. The nearest thing this base holds is shipped puzzle mi-9f06a55404, where Qxf8+ forces Rxf8 and exf8=Q is mate — and it is NOT filed here, because sources are divided on whether that combination is a decoy or a deflection and `themesOf()` refuses to name either. A motif label the base cannot defend is worse than a missing example.

NO AMBIGUOUS EXAMPLE, and the reason is the order of the work rather than a shortage of positions. This record has no POSITIVE example either, and an ambiguous example is a position where the concept is genuinely present and what to conclude from it is unclear - which cannot be written before there is an agreed instance of the concept being present at all. The four motifs in this base that lack a positive - `clearance`, `decoy`, `deflection`, `interference` - lack it for reasons written on each record, and the ambiguous rung waits on that. Writing one first would be asserting a doubtful instance of something this base has not yet shown a clear instance of.

examples.note: Anderssen-Dufresne, Berlin 1852, 21.Qxd7+ - the queen sacrifice that lures the king to d7, where the double check 22.Bf5+ works and the mate follows. This is this record's FIRST positive example. It has carried a limitation saying it had none, and the reason given there was that four constructions had failed and the base's nearest candidate was a combination sources call a deflection as often as a decoy. This one is the textbook form: a piece is not being pulled off a duty, it is being pulled ONTO a square, and the square is d7 because that is where the rook on d1 and a bishop can check at the same time. Mate in 4. PROVENANCE. The move list was replayed through this base's own move generator by tools/replay_game.js, which refuses a wrong list rather than guessing, so the FEN is verified rather than remembered. No named annotator is attached to this position for this concept, so it grounds the MASTER-GAME rung and not the human-grounded one.

engine.verdict_note: Mate in 4 at depth 20, settled at depth 1, and the sacrifice is the engine's first choice. The whole line is forced: Qxd7+ Kxd7 Bf5+ Ke8 Bd7+ Kf8 Bxe7#.

counterexamples.note: Registered false-positive case `a-king-decoyed-to-safety`, kept on the record as well as in tests/false_positive_cases.json so that the concept carries its own negative evidence. THE SURFACE PATTERN IS PRESENT: Ra8+ forces the black king to move to h7 — a check that must be answered by a king move to a specific square is exactly how a decoy operates. WHY IT IS NOT THE CONCEPT: Nothing is waiting on h7. A decoy lures a piece ONTO a square where a tactic works against it — a fork square, a mating square, a line where a pin or skewer becomes available — and White has a rook and three pawns. The king is forced to a square and the square is safe. WHAT THE SYSTEM DOES: The API reports `open-file` and nothing else; `decoy` has no matcher and this record's limitations say why — the motif is 'only identifiable by looking at the resulting position, so it cannot be detected from the move alone'. This case is the cheap version of that: forcing a king to a square is mechanical and trivial to detect, and it is the half of the concept that carries none of the meaning. The position is dead level.

by_level.beginner: This offers something to pull the enemy piece onto a square where you can win it or give mate.
by_level.intermediate: A decoy: the sacrifice drags the {piece} onto {square}, where {follow-up} wins.
by_level.advanced: Decoy / attraction (Informant theme h). Verify the follow-up exists and that the offer cannot be declined.
